$comment: Field-guide text for the animal dialog. Facts are general natural-history statements about the real animal, written for this game. Roles and lifespans that depend on the model are derived from species.json and food-web.json at runtime, not written here.

rabbit.habitat: Open grassland and field edges, close to cover such as hedges, scrub and burrows.
rabbit.diet: Grass, herbs and clover, plus bark and shoots in winter. Rabbits digest tough plant fibre partly by eating their own soft droppings a second time.
rabbit.behaviour: Most active at dusk and dawn. Feeds in the open but runs to cover at the first sign of danger.
facts: Rabbits eat their own soft droppings, called caecotrophs, to take in nutrients they missed the first time round. It is normal behaviour.
A rabbit's teeth never stop growing, so it has to gnaw constantly to wear them down.
A rabbit has almost all-round vision, with a small blind spot directly in front of its nose.
A rabbit warns others of danger by thumping a hind foot on the ground.
Rabbits are most active at dusk and dawn. The name for this kind of timing is crepuscular.
Wild rabbits often live in burrow systems called warrens, which can be used by many generations.
Rabbits breed fast. Gestation is about a month, and a doe can have several litters in a season.

cow.habitat: Pasture and meadows with a reliable water supply. Herds graze together and rest in the same places.
cow.diet: Grass and other plants. Cows have a four-chambered stomach, and microbes in the first chamber, the rumen, break down the cellulose in plant fibre.
cow.behaviour: Social animals with stable herd bonds. Grazes for several hours a day and chews the cud while resting.
facts: Cows chew the cud: they bring food back up from the first stomach chamber and chew it again.
The rumen holds many litres of food and is full of microbes. The cow cannot digest cellulose without them.
A cow's pregnancy lasts about nine months. A newborn calf usually stands within about an hour.
Cows form close friendships within a herd, and they can become stressed when separated from companions.
A dairy cow can drink more than 100 litres of water a day in hot weather.
Grazing removes grass faster than it can regrow when too many animals share one patch. That leaves bare ground.

chicken.habitat: Farmyards, hedgerows and open ground with cover for roosting at night.
chicken.diet: Seeds, grain, green shoots, insects and worms. Chickens are omnivores.
chicken.behaviour: Scratches the ground with its feet to uncover seeds and insects. Roosts on perches at night.
facts: Domestic chickens are descended from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia.
Chickens can see ultraviolet light, which helps them pick out seeds and feathers.
Chickens roost high at night, which keeps them out of reach of foxes and other ground hunters.
Chickens can fly short distances to escape or reach a roost, but they cannot sustain long flights.
Modern laying hens can produce roughly 250 to 300 eggs a year.
A chicken scratches the ground to uncover food. This also loosens the soil.

mouse.habitat: Hedges, field edges, woodland floors and buildings. Stays in dense cover where it can hide.
mouse.diet: Seeds, grain, fruit and insects. Mice are omnivores, but seeds make up most of their food in the wild.
mouse.behaviour: Forages mostly at night, follows the same runs through cover, and freezes or bolts when threatened.
facts: A house mouse can squeeze through a gap about 6 mm wide, roughly the thickness of a pencil.
Mice breed very quickly. A female can have a new litter every few weeks in good conditions.
Mice find their way with whiskers and smell, and they keep to familiar runs.
A mouse's pregnancy lasts about three weeks.
Mice rely on cover such as long grass and hedges. Open ground exposes them to hunters.
A mouse can get most of the water it needs from the seeds it eats.

fox.habitat: Woodland edges, hedgerows, farmland and towns. Needs cover and somewhere to den.
fox.diet: Mainly small mammals such as mice and rabbits, plus birds, insects, fruit and carrion. Foxes take whatever food is easiest to find.
fox.behaviour: Usually hunts alone, mostly at dusk and at night. Rests and raises young in dens called earths.
facts: A fox hunting small rodents often listens for them, then pounces and lands on the prey hidden under grass or snow.
A red fox can run at speeds up to about 48 km/h over short distances.
Foxes communicate with a wide range of sounds, including barks and screams.
A fox often buries spare food and returns to it later.
Cubs are born in spring, usually in litters of four to six.
Foxes defend a home range with borders they mark. Neighbouring foxes usually keep to their own ground.
A fox needs enough prey to live on. In this model a population of foxes falls quickly when rabbits and mice decline.
